Linear model is done by adding the input in which each is multiplied by a learned weight,
y = w0x0 + w1x1 + ... + wpxp + b where w=learned-weight x=input, b = bias(intercept)
weight measures how important each feature is if w (=+) feature increases, (=-) decreases  (=0) doesnt matter to the prediction

linear regression makes prediction by using straignt line relationship between features and target 1 feature means 1 prediction line 2 features plane 3+ features hyperplane produces straight flat shapes no curves.
KNeighborsRegressor → wiggly, flexible curve, Linear Regression → straight line

The more features the more linear regression becomes powerful because it changes from line to plane to hyperplane that cuts through data in complex ways if you have more features than training samples, a linear model can fit the training data perfectly.

All linear regression uses the same formula but differ in how they learn weights and control complexity e.g ordinary least squares(ols) no complexity control, it chooses weight and bias that minimize 

Ridge regression prevents weight from becoming too large by keeping value close to the training data. Small weight means each feature has less influence, model is simpler and less likely to overfit. It uses L2 regularization that penalizes large weights
lasso can force some weights to become zero. it is an alternative to ridge that regularize linear regression it uses l1 regularization and forces some coefficent equal to zero. Meaning some features are ignored since they sere set to zero. it selects the most important features and ignore the rest

Elastic net a mixture of ridge and lasso

Regularization mean adding a rule that prevents the model from becoming complex, ridge uses L2 regularization that penalizes large weights.
It is useful for many features, noisy data, correlated features


linear classifier tries to seperate two classes using a straight line(2D), a plane in 3D, hyperplane in hihger dimensions
w0x0 + w1x1 + ... + wpxp, if res>0 predicts class +1, if res <0 predicts class -1 =0 boundary such as line plane hyperplane 

Linear regression(is a linear function of features lines, plane, hyperplane) vs linear classification(decision boundary is a linear function of input)
LR output is a number LC output is a class, LR draws a line or plane that fits data Lc draws a line or plane that seperates class

LC types include Logistic Regression uses the logistic*sigmund function produces probability 
linear SVM uses hinge loss focus on maximizing the margin producing sharper boundaries 

Both are linear classifiers, they try to find a straight line that best separates the classes, so their boundaries often look almost identical.
Both misclassify two points, because the forge dataset is not perfectly linearly separable. 
C controls how strict the model is about fitting the training data.
High C, Less regularization Model tries very hard to classify every point correctly, Decision boundary may bend closer to outliers
Low C, More regularization, Model prefers simpler coefficients (closer to zero) ignores outliers, Decision boundary becomes smoother

Small C → simple model → small coefficients → sometimes wrong sign Large C → complex model → large coefficients → more sensitive to noise
Sign flips show that coefficient interpretation is unstable

most linear models (Linear SVM, Linear Regression)are built for binary classification to handle more than one we use One vs Rest Trick
we make a class into binary eg K-class classifier 1: A or nor A, classifier 2: B or not B etc.
when a new points comes in each classifier computes a score, the score tells how strongly the model believes the point belongs to the class
whichever classifier has the highest score wins, Winner takes all

linear model has one big parameter that controls how complex the model is 
α (alpha) → used in regression models (Ridge, Lasso), C → used in classification models (LinearSVC, LogisticRegression) 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100

Large α or small C → strong regularization → simpler model, Small α or large C → weak regularization → more complex model,  
Strong regularization = “keep weights small, avoid overfitting”, Weak regularization = “fit the data more closely, even if weights get large”

Choosing L1 vs L2 regularization: If you want (feature selection → choose L1), (stability and general performance → choose L2)
L2  Default choice, Spreads weight across many features, Stable and works well in most cases
L1 Makes many weights exactly zero, Useful when: You believe only a few features matter You want interpretability (easy to see which features are used)

merits of linear Model: Fast to train, predict, Works well with sparse data
demerits: Hard to interpret when features are correlated, Not great in low-dimensional spaces, If  true boundary is curved or complex, linear models struggle.

Native Bayes is one of the simplest ML classfiers. It predicts a class by calculating how likely each class is given the features
assuming each feature works independently Naive(all features are independent of each other)
it checks how often a feature appear in a class, for new data it check which class is most probable with the features picks class with highest probability

Types of Naive Bayes in scikit-learn 
GaussianNB for continous features assume features follows a gaussian(normal distribution) stores mean standard deviation for each feature per class
Bernoulli binary(0/1) features used mostly in text classification(presence or absence of words) counts how many features is non zero per class
MultinominalNB Count data(how many times a word appears) or text classification stores average counts per feature per class

merits of NB: Text classification (spam, sentiment, topic detection), Very high-dimensional data, When speed matters, When training data is huge
demerits f NB: Independence assumption is unrealistic → slightly worse accuracy than logistic regression or SVM 
Not great when features interact strongly, GaussianNB struggles if data is not normally distributed

Count how often each feature appears in each class → use those counts to guess the class,  smart counting + probability

Decision tree is a Ml model that makes prediction by asking a series of yes or no questions
A series of question is asked depending on answer to ask the next question and move forward backward left or right until the final destination

A decision tree builds itself by repeatedly choosing the best yes/no question that splits the data into purer groups. 
For continuous features, the questions are of the form “Is feature i ≤ value?”. 
The tree chooses the split that best separates the classes, creates two new regions, and repeats the process in each region until the data is well separated.

Decision Trees grow using a recursive process (The tree keeps repeating the same step over and over)
Pick the best yes/no question - Split the data - Go to each side - Repeat the process again - Stop when the data is clean
this repeated splitting creates a binary tree (each node has two branches: yes or no)

Decision trees only ask questions about one feature at a time, like: Is x[0] ≤ 1.5?
Because each question uses one feature, the splits are always straight vertical or horizontal lines, called axis‑parallel boundaries.
The tree is building a “hierarchical partition like: Region A: Sub A  Region B and keeps splitting until each region is pure
A region (leaf) is pure when: All the points inside it belong to the same class. Leaf 1 → all points are class 0 Leaf 2 → all points are class 1

why decision Tree becomes too complex 
it will perfectly memorize the training data perform accurately on training data but poorly on new data, causing overfitting
A pure leaf means all point in that leaf belong to the same class 
Sounds good, but is actually bad because the tree starts creating tiny regions just to fit outliers.

How to prevent overfitting
Pre pruning (stop early) 
Max_depth limit how many split the tree can take, max_leaf_nodes: limit how many leaves it can create, 
min_smaple_split: require a minimum number of points before splitting min_smaple_leave:  require a minimum number of points in leaves
Post‑pruning (cut back later)
Let the tree grow fully, then remove branches that don’t help.

Which features the decision tree used the most to make decisions. Every feature gets a score between 0 and 1:
0 → the tree never used this feature Higher number → the feature was used more often and made bigger splits All importances add up to 1
feature importance is basically: How much each feature contributed to splitting the data. some have 0 becuase they were never used in any split

How much each feature contributed to splitting the data.

pruning reduce the size of the tree by removing branches that has little to no predictive power making the model simple
and more generalizable.

pre pruning stopping the growth eaerly by removing branches using max_depth to state how may questions should be asked or 
require a minimum number of samples to split (min_samples_split) require a minimum number of samples per leaf (min_samples_leaf)

First grow the tree fully (allowing overfitting). Then cut back branches that don’t improve performance on a validation set.

Normal plt.plot(): Both axes are linear.
plt.semilogy(): The x-axis is linear, but the y-axis uses a log scale.
plt.semilogx(): The opposite — x-axis is logarithmic, y-axis is linear.
plt.loglog(): Both axes are logarithmic.
